# 1. Reproduce the bug deterministically first — write a minimal failing test case before changing any code.
# 2. Read the full traceback bottom-up: the last frame shows where the error occurred, earlier frames show how you got there.
# 3. Insert `breakpoint()` (Python 3.7+) to drop into pdb and inspect live variable states instead of guessing.
# 4. Log intermediate values with `logging.debug()` rather than `print()`, so you can toggle verbosity without editing code.
# 5. Bisect the problem: use `git bisect` or comment out code halves to find the exact commit or line that introduced the failure.
# 6. Verify your type assumptions — many bugs come from `str` vs `bytes`, `int` vs `float`, or a `None` sneaking into a variable.
# 7. Check classic Python pitfalls: mutable default arguments (`def f(x=[])`), off-by-one slice bounds, and shadowed variable names.
# 8. Add `assert` statements for invariants during development so failures point to the violated assumption immediately.
# 9. Strip the failing case down to the smallest reproducible example — deleting unrelated code often makes the root cause obvious.
# 10. Explain the code line-by-line out loud (rubber-duck debugging); verbalizing logic frequently exposes the flawed assumption.
